title: Guaranteed Basic Income, Mental Health, and Substance-Use-Attributable Harms in an AI-Driven Economy: A Canadian Threshold Cost–Benefit Analysis
content: Income-security interventions may improve mental health and reduce substance-related harms, but effect sizes remain uncertain. This study develops a Canadian threshold cost–benefit model of guaranteed basic income during AI-related labour-market disruption. Using observed productivity losses and a comorbidity adjustment, it estimates an annual burden of CAN$38.44 billion. Compared with annual gross program expenditure of CAN$87.57 billion, the maximum productivity-benefit ratio is 0.439, and break-even requires a 227.8% reduction. This is a program-scale benchmark, not a social benefit–cost ratio. When cost is represented by the excess burden of taxation using marginal costs of public funds of 1.2–1.3, the illustrative break-even reduction falls to 45.6%–68.3%, excluding administrative costs. An 8.5% reduction, retained only for comparison with Manitoba MINCOME, yields a gross-expenditure ratio of 0.037. Mortality is evaluated separately: 234,597 statistical life-years would need to be gained annually to equal gross expenditure. These are conditional thresholds, not causal estimates.
